stated_availability: Descriptive only (not mapped to L1-L6). No dedicated Data Availability Statement in the article. Availability signals are: (1) Appendix A, p. 18: "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921."; (2) Section 2.3.3, p. 4: "All analyses were undertaken in 'R' version 4.3.0. The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information."; (3) Section 2.4, p. 6: "The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information."; (4) title page licence: "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)." No repository name, dataset DOI, accession, or code repository URL is given anywhere; no statement is made about deposition of the underlying record-level morphometric data, which the paper attributes to prior publications, monographs, unpublished theses, and co-author-held collections.

F1.evidence: No dataset-level persistent identifier. The only identifier offered for supplementary content is the article's own DOI: 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921' (Appendix A, p. 18). That DOI identifies the article record, not a data resource; no dataset DOI, accession, IGSN, or repository identifier appears in the paper.

F2.evidence: No structured metadata record exists for any data resource. Datasets are described only in narrative Methods and in-article table captions (e.g. Table 1, p. 6, 'Descriptive morphometric data for the two replica stone tool assemblages used in the validation analyses'). There is no repository landing page, DataCite record, README, or data dictionary evidenced; supplementary items are referenced only by number ('Supplementary Tables 1 and 2', 'Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2').

F3.evidence: Unscoreable and therefore 0: with no dataset metadata record (F2 = 0) there is no metadata in which an identifier could be embedded. The paper carries no data-level identifier at all.

F4.evidence: No data are registered or indexed in a searchable data registry. No Zenodo, figshare, Dryad, tDAR, Open Context, or DataCite deposit is named; only the article itself is indexed (ScienceDirect/Crossref). The paper names no repository whatsoever.

A1.evidence: A1 = 0 by the instrument's completeness rule: data_completeness coverage_category is 'minimal' (3 of 14 datasets at Tier 0-2, 21.4%). Record-level data are never stated as deposited; the majority route to a closed monograph ('measured using diameter boards ... (see: Petrie, 2020)', Section 2.4.4.1, p. 8; 'following Robb (2007)', Section 2.4.4.2), unpublished theses ('The methods used to collect these data have been previously described in Martin-Ramos (2022)', Section 2.4.1.3, p. 7, referenced as 'Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London'; Fig. 6 caption cites eight assemblages from 'Key (2015)', an 'Unpublished PhD Thesis, University of Kent'), or co-author-held material ('the specimens have since been curated at the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory', Section 2.3.2, p. 4). No ethical or legal restriction is claimed anywhere, so the exception does not apply.

A1_1.evidence: For the accessible portion, the protocol is open, free, and universally implementable: the article is gold open access ('This is an open access article under the CC BY license', p. 1) and its supplementary material resolves over HTTPS from the article DOI (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921, Appendix A, p. 18) with no paywall, login, or proprietary client. The three upstream datasets classified Tier 2 likewise sit behind open-access articles.

A1_2.evidence: No authentication/authorisation procedure is documented, and no ethically or legally justified restricted-access pathway exists (no CARE, human-subjects, or heritage-sensitivity restriction is invoked anywhere in the paper). The inaccessible majority of the research data is closed by default - closed monographs, unpublished theses, and co-author holdings - with no governed access route stated, which is 'completely closed with no justification' rather than governed restriction.

A2.evidence: No commitment to persistence of data metadata independent of the data themselves. There is no repository record (Zenodo/DANS/domain repository) and no dataset metadata to persist; supplementary files are attached to the article with no separate metadata object. Consistent with F2 = F3 = 0: metadata that does not exist cannot persist.

I1.evidence: No machine-actionable data representation is evidenced. Data reach the reader as typeset PDF tables of summary statistics (Table 1 p. 6; Tables 5-7 pp. 12-13, e.g. Table 5 'Range data for each morphological variable investigated for each artefact case study') plus unnamed, unspecified-format 'Supplementary Tables'. No CSV/JSON/XML file, schema, or structured data package is named; per the FAIR guide, PDF/table-in-article delivery is available but not machine-actionable.

I2.evidence: No FAIR vocabularies or controlled terminologies are used for the data. Artefact typologies and periods are free text with literature citations ('Clovis, Eastern Clovis, Folsom and Midland point types', Section 2.4.1.5, p. 7; 'Impressed Ware' and 'Stentinello' styles, Section 2.4.4.2, p. 8) with no PeriodO, Getty AAT, CIDOC-CRM, or ARIADNEplus URIs anywhere.

I3.evidence: No qualified, typed, machine-readable references from a data resource to other resources. Provenance links exist only as prose citations in the article body (e.g. 'Data are derived from Buchanan and Hamilton's (2021) study of scaling laws in Paleoindian points', Section 2.4.1.5, p. 7); because no dataset metadata record exists, there is nothing carrying typed relations such as 'isDerivedFrom' with resolvable PIDs.

R1.evidence: The datasets are richly described in the article with a plurality of relevant attributes: sample sizes, variables, units, and definitions (Table 1, p. 6, gives mean, SD, CV, minimum and maximum for length, breadth, thickness, mass, elongation, refinement, PC1, PC2, with footnote '*Refinement is used here to describe the relative thickness of a tool (thickness divided by breadth)'), plus site, chronology, and material context for every case study (e.g. 'Howiesons Poort bipolar cores from Sibudu Cave (South Africa, 63.8 +/- 2.5 ka)', p. 5) and measurement methods by citation ('Flake length (mm), width (mm), thickness (mm) and mass (g) are investigated and recorded using the methods in Key et al. (2022)', Section 2.4.1.1, p. 6).

R1_1.evidence: A clear, accessible, machine-readable usage licence covers the published article and its accompanying supplementary material: '0305-4403/(c) 2023 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (p. 1). SPDX equivalent CC-BY-4.0, with resolvable licence URI. No separate, conflicting data licence is asserted.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance is documented for the datasets: creation events and dates ('500 replica Acheulean handaxes were produced by Key and Lycett (2017) on British flint over the course of 18 months', Section 2.3.1, p. 4; the Early Archaic points 'were originally knapped by M.I.E. in 2021 with the intention of conducting a ballistics experiment involving their breakage', Section 2.3.2, p. 4), excavation provenance ('is part of a larger LCT assemblage from Olduvai Gorge Beds III and IV (ca.1300-600 ka) excavated by Mary Leakey and colleagues between the 1960 and 1971 (n = 562)', Section 2.4.1.3, p. 7), and processing/transformation steps ('duplicates were automatically removed before the validation analyses', Section 2.3.1, p. 4; 'we resampled each value from a normal distribution, where we used the value itself as the mean, and a very small standard deviation (0.001). We repeated the OLE procedure with randomised values for 1000 iterations', Section 2.4.1.6.1, p. 8), plus the analysis environment ('R' version 4.3.0, Section 2.3.3, p. 4).

R1_3.evidence: No domain-relevant data or metadata community standard is applied. There is no Dublin Core, DataCite, ARIADNEplus, CIDOC-CRM, tDAR, or Open Context conformance; measurement conventions are followed by citation to individual prior papers ('following the method outlined by de la Pena and Wadley (2014)', Section 2.4.1.4, p. 7) rather than to a community data standard, and no standard-conformant data file is deposited.

F1.evidence: No software persistent identifier. Code is located only by prose: 'The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information' (Section 2.3.3, p. 4) and 'The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information' (Section 2.4, p. 6). No Zenodo DOI, SWHID, CRAN entry, or even a GitHub URL appears; the supplement is reachable only via the article DOI (10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921), which identifies the publication, not the software.

F2.evidence: No structured software metadata. No CodeMeta.json, CITATION.cff, DESCRIPTION file, or repository record is evidenced or named; the scripts are referred to generically as 'The script', with no title, version, author list, or dependency description as a metadata object.

F3.evidence: Unscoreable and therefore 0: no software metadata record exists (F2 = 0), so no metadata can carry a software identifier. No code-level identifier of any kind is stated in the paper.

F4.evidence: The code is not registered or indexed in any searchable software registry. No Zenodo, Software Heritage, CRAN, JOSS, or institutional software catalogue is named; the scripts exist only as undifferentiated files attached to the article record.

A1.evidence: The complete analysis code is claimed to be retrievable via a standard protocol: both scripts are stated to be supplied - 'The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information' (Section 2.3.3, p. 4) and 'The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information' (Section 2.4, p. 6) - and supplementary material resolves over HTTPS from the article DOI ('Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105921', Appendix A, p. 18). Both the validation and case-study components of the paper's computation are covered by the two stated scripts.

A1_1.evidence: Retrieval is by open, free, universally implementable protocol: the article is open access under CC BY ('This is an open access article under the CC BY license', p. 1), so the supplementary scripts download over plain HTTPS with no subscription, registration, or proprietary client.

A1_2.evidence: No authentication or authorisation procedure is documented for the code, and no restriction requiring one is asserted (no proprietary dependency, embargo, or sensitivity claim). Nothing in the paper evidences a governed access route, so this sub-principle is unscoreable and scores 0.

A2.evidence: No persistence commitment for software metadata independent of the files. The code is not archived in Software Heritage or Zenodo and has no metadata record that would survive removal of the supplementary files; there is no tombstone or registry entry for the scripts.

I1.evidence: The code uses a formal, accessible, shared, and broadly applicable representation: 'All analyses were undertaken in "R" version 4.3.0' (Section 2.3.3, p. 4). R is an open, standard, non-proprietary scripting language, and the named version pins the interpreter, satisfying the standard-format criterion for software.

I2.evidence: No FAIR vocabularies, ontologies, or standardised schemas are used by or declared for the code; no controlled vocabulary is applied to variables, parameters, or outputs anywhere in the paper.

I3.evidence: No qualified, PID-bearing references from the software to other resources. Dependencies are not enumerated (no package list, no version pins beyond the R interpreter, no renv.lock or requirements file), and the methodological ancestry is given only as prose citations ('The formulaic expression of OLE is widely available through open-access sources (e.g., Pimiento and Clements, 2014; Roberts et al., 2021; Key et al., 2021b)', Section 2.1, p. 2) rather than typed machine-readable links.

R1.evidence: The computation the scripts implement is richly described with a plurality of relevant attributes: model, parameters, and run configuration are specified - 'we use the 10 (k) largest or smallest measurements of a given trait ... we also assessed the use of k values of 5, 20 and 30 for all validation tests' and 'randomly sampled subsamples were then entered into the OLE model ... One thousand iterations of each process were performed for all subsampling percentages and k, and results were presented as median values across all iterations' (Sections 2.3.3 and 2.3.1, p. 4), plus the duplicate-handling and resampling procedure (Section 2.4.1.6.1, p. 8) and the interpreter version (R 4.3.0).

R1_1.evidence: A clear, accessible usage licence covers the article and the supplementary scripts distributed with it: '(c) 2023 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (p. 1), i.e. CC-BY-4.0 with a resolvable licence URI. No separate or more restrictive code licence is asserted.

R1_2.evidence: Provenance for the code does not go beyond authorship plus the interpreter version. The CRediT statement (p. 18) allocates roles ('Alastair Key: Conceptualization, Data curation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Methodology, Validation, Writing - original draft ...'), and R 4.3.0 is named, but there is no software version, release date, changelog, version-control history, dependency provenance, or random-seed documentation for the stochastic 1000-iteration subsampling. Authorship alone does not meet the detailed-provenance bar.

R1_3.evidence: No software community standard is met: no CITATION.cff or CodeMeta, no CRAN/rOpenSci packaging, no container or environment specification, no test suite, no installation instructions. The code is delivered as loose scripts in a journal supplement with no conformance statement.

barriers: No record-level data deposit stated anywhere: the only availability claims cover scripts ('The script used to run all validation analyses is available in the supplementary information', Section 2.3.3, p. 4; 'The script used to run all case study tests is available in the supplementary information', Section 2.4, p. 6); in-article tables give summary statistics only

Closed monograph: Middle Historic ceramic bowls from the Bannu Basin (rim diameter n = 1466) measured 'using diameter boards with 1 cm increments, callipers and a metal rule (see: Petrie, 2020)' - Petrie 2020, Oxbow Books (Tier 3)
Closed monograph: Neolithic Impressed Ware and Stentinello pots investigated 'following Robb (2007)' - Robb 2007, Cambridge University Press (Tier 3)
Unpublished thesis: Olduvai Bed III/IV cleavers (n = 134), methods 'previously described in Martin-Ramos (2022)', referenced as 'Unpublished PhD thesis. University College London' (Tier 3)
Unpublished thesis: eight additional Acheulean handaxe assemblages in Fig. 6C 'previously analysed by Key (2015)', referenced as 'Unpublished PhD Thesis, University of Kent' (Tier 3)

Co-author gatekeeping / unpublished: replica Early Archaic points (n = 45) which 'have not been used in any other published studies' and whose 'specimens have since been curated at the Kent State University Experimental Archaeology Laboratory' (Section 2.3.2, p. 4) (Tier 3)
Co-author gatekeeping: copper socketed tang points (n = 93) - no data source or deposit cited for the length, breadth, thickness and mass measurements (Section 2.4.3.1, p. 8) (Tier 3)

Co-author gatekeeping / paywall: replica handaxe assemblage (n = 500) and Boxgrove handaxes (n = 254), for which only 'The methods used to collect these data can be viewed in Key and Lycett (2017)' is offered (Sections 2.3.1 and 2.4.1.2) (Tier 3)

Paywall with no deposit stated: Sibudu bipolar cores (n = 131), data 'recorded from each core following the method outlined by de la Pena and Wadley (2014)' (Section 2.4.1.4) and Cueva de la Cocina geometric microliths (n = 734) per Cortell-Nicolau et al. (2023) / Cortell-Nicolau (2019) (Tier 3)

Manual extraction required for the accessible minority: the three Tier 2 datasets (Old Park flakes n = 173 via Key et al. 2022 RSOS; Paleoindian points n = 1281 via Buchanan and Hamilton 2021 Sci. Rep.; capuchin flakes n = 31 via Proffitt et al. 2016 Nature) must be chased through third-party article supplements rather than retrieved from this paper
Sensitivity note: even a maximally generous reclassification counting every journal-article-sourced dataset as Tier 2 yields 7/14 = 50%, still 'partial', so data A1 = 0 either way
